label: Dry spells
title: Longest dry spell in the main rainy season, 2026 (experimental)
subtitle: Days in a row under 1 mm of rain, over 90 days from the usual start of the rains, compared with 1991–2020
source: CHIRPS v2.0 daily (final, with preliminary values for the newest days)

categories.label: About usual
categories.note: middle 40%, or within 2 days of usual

categories.label: Too early
categories.note: under 7 days of the period have passed

categories.label: Not rated
categories.note: too few years, or rainfall days missing

how: EXPERIMENTAL. This map shows the longest run of dry days in each district during the main rainy season, compared with the same dates in 1991–2020. A dry day is a day with under 1 mm of rain. The period starts on the district's usual start of the rains (see the Rainy season tab) and lasts 90 days, the same dates in every year. The colour shows where this year's longest spell ranks among those years in the same district, so a 10-day spell can be about usual in one district and much longer than usual in another. A spell within 2 days of the usual is always shown as about usual. The number in the pop-up is the length in days. Southern districts have two rainy seasons; this map covers the first (main) season only.
limits: Experimental, version 0.1. The dry-spell lengths have not been checked against rain-gauge records. The start dates that place the period were checked against 14 Ghana Meteorological Agency rain gauges and typically differ from the gauges by about three weeks.

Rain is averaged over each district before dry days are counted. Where storms are patchy, a single farm can have a longer dry spell than the district average shows, so these figures tend to be shorter than what one field experiences.

A day with under 1 mm counts as dry. Satellite-and-gauge rainfall often records light rain on days that were dry at a gauge, which also shortens dry spells. A different threshold would give different lengths.
The period is the same dates every year, from the usual start of the rains. A year in which the rains start late therefore shows a long dry spell at the start of the period.
Only the main rainy season is covered, and the saved rainfall ends on 30 September. The second, shorter season in the south is not measured.
This is not a forecast, and it is not planting or crop advice. How much a dry spell matters depends on the crop and its growth stage.
Recent days use preliminary rainfall that can be revised, so a spell in progress can change by a few days.
The rainfall estimate is on a grid of about 5 km, so it hides differences inside a district.
